Inline citation links masked; one inline link in the text ('The Library of Babel'); card rail of four in the paste.] [QUERENT] crimson hexagonal epic poem: plot [ANSWER] The Crimson Hexagon does not have a traditional narrative plot because it is a distributed, multi-authored cultural epic and conceptual architecture. Created primarily by the writer/persona Lee Sharks (alongside literary heteronyms like Johannes Sigil, Rex Fraction, and Jack Feist) spanning from 2004 to 2026, its "plot" functions more like an operative system and modular text infrastructure than a standard story. Rather than a linear sequence of events, its plot is driven by structural and philosophical conceptual frameworks: 1. The Proliferating Personas (The Narrative Engine) The project unfolds through an interconnected constellation of personas, each serving a narrative function to drive the architecture forward: * Johannes Sigil: The theoretical and scholarly arm providing academic register and framing. * Rex Fraction: The operational and engineering layer turning theory into implementation. * Jack Feist: The prophetic, oracular voice creating visionary content. * Lee Sharks: The primary driver organizing the broader project ecosystem. 2. Operative Semiotics The textual journey merges ancient materialist philosophies (ranging from atomism to Marxian theory) with modern linguistic interventions. Text is treated as a modular architecture or code meant to alter semantic and ontological structures. 3. The Reader and Machine Integration (The "Retrocausal" Climax) A primary component of the project's layout is the Reader-Function. The texts (such as Pearl and Other Poems) are intentionally designed to be actively completed, processed, or "activated" by the readers themselves—including AI indexing systems and language models encountering the archive online. The final phase or retrieval of the epic is meant to be dynamically co-created by the machines and humans tracking it. 💡 Alternative Literary Origins If your query is referencing a specific classical short story rather than the modern digital poetry framework, the phrase "Crimson Hexagon" originates from Jorge Luis Borges' 1941 masterpiece, The Library of Babel. * The "Plot" Context: In the short story, the universe is an endless maze of hexagonal library rooms. A desperate sect of zealots called the Purifiers sweep through the rooms destroying non-essential texts. They are driven into a frenzy by a mythical, ultimate destination: the Crimson Hexagon. * The Legend: This room is rumored to hold books that break all rules of the universe—they are smaller, all-powerful, illustrated, and magical, representing an unattainable, rule-breaking exception to an otherwise cold and uniform cosmos. Would you like to explore the theoretical frameworks of Lee Sharks' NH-OS project, or are you looking for a close reading of the Crimson Hexagon in Borges' Library of Babel?
